summary: AE + SE from Redwood and PeakAnalytics scoped the POC benchmark integration. Discussed workload sizing (QPS, concurrency), streaming vs non-streaming scenarios, harness repo, security/VPC access, and success criteria (latency SLO, throughput targets, cost per 1M tokens). Agreed next steps to exchange artifacts, set up staging credentials, and run a 2-hour benchmark next week.
topics: Security / VPC access and data handling
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-05
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (PeakAnalytics Head of ML), Priya Kumar (Platform Eng), Aaron Lee (SRE)
Artifacts referenced: Redwood benchmark harness repo (internal link placeholder: https://repo.redwood.internal/bench-harness), sample prompt set (drive link), security questionnaire (doc link)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intros - i'm Maya, AE on the account, with Liam, our SE. Jordan, do you want to kick off with what you're trying to validate in the POC?

[00:22] Jordan Reyes: Yeah sure. We're looking to validate throughput and cost for our customer-facing generation pipeline. Key metrics are p95 latency under 500ms for short prompts (~128 tokens), and throughput of roughly 200 qps for non-streaming requests, and then also evaluate streaming path for multi-turn chat. We want to know cost per million tokens and failure modes under load.

[00:50] Liam O'Connor: ok got it. When you say 200 qps, is that concurrent or sustained? and what's your average sequence length?

[01:05] Jordan Reyes: 200 sustained during business hours, spikes to 400 for a few minutes. average generation is 128 tokens, some long tails at 512. concurrency wise we expect ~50 concurrent streams during the 400 spike.

[01:30] Priya Kumar: from platform side we care about networking and whether the benchmark can run inside our VPC. we can't expose data, so we'll need ephemeral test keys and maybe a VPC peering or private link.

[01:45] Maya Chen: makes sense. For the harness we typically support both remote (hosted API) and private deployment benchmarks. We'll share the harness repo which includes k6/gatling scripts and a runner for streaming vs non-streaming. Note: the repo README has example configs for QPS, concurrency and sequence length.

[02:10] Aaron Lee: quick question — streaming is tricky for us because we currently use SSE and websockets in prod. how does Redwood's streaming behave under sustained concurrency?

[02:28] Liam O'Connor: good callout. streaming keeps an open connection per session so resource usage is different — CPU and connection limits matter more than per-token compute. For the POC we'll run two passes: non-streaming batch requests to measure throughput/cost, and a streaming pass to measure connection scaling, p95 of first-byte and tail latency. We'll also do prefix caching tests to see win on repeated prompts.

[03:05] Jordan Reyes: ok, what about warmup? KV cache behavior? our workloads have a lot of similar prefixes.

[03:18] Liam O'Connor: the harness can simulate realistic reuse with seed prompt pools. we can hit with a workload shaped to your distribution — warmup for 10-15 minutes, then ramp to targets. We'll also run a cold-start baseline. I should warn that some internal names in the repo are auto generated, sometimes transcribed as 'Redwoo Dedicate' in notes but it's Redwood Dedicated.

[03:45] Priya Kumar: on security — do you have SOC2 docs and a KMS integration for private deployments? We need to know data is not persisted in your hosted flows.

[03:58] Maya Chen: yes. we have SOC2 and ISO artifacts and KMS/HSM support for Private. For the hosted POC we'll provide SOC2 summary and an encrypted channel, and for Dedicated/Private we can do KMS key control. we'll send the questionnaire answers after this call.

[04:20] Aaron Lee: Great. on the harness side, what do you need from us?

[04:30] Liam O'Connor: sample prompt set, what portion of prompts are multi-turn streaming vs single-shot non-streaming, expected QPS distribution, and access to a staging environment in your VPC or test subnet. ideally a small dataset we can use for tokenization and to measure RLHF-like multi-turn behavior.

[04:55] Jordan Reyes: we can provide that — i'll export our canonical prompt set (~2k prompts) and a script that wraps our business logic. we prefer to run the harness from within our infra to avoid egress and to validate networking.

[05:12] Maya Chen: perfect. We'll support both approaches: Redwood can run the harness from our staging (hosted) and also provide instructions to run inside your VPC using our agent. For inside-VPC runs we'll need temporary test credentials and a whitelisted IP/subnet.

[05:34] Priya Kumar: what about the load generator — do you recommend k6 or something else? we run locust internally.

[05:44] Liam O'Connor: k6 is what we include by default but we have translation examples for locust and gatling. The important part is the request shape (headers, streaming vs not, stream chunk cadence). We'll hand over a locust config if you prefer.

[06:05] Jordan Reyes: can you walk through the success criteria you generally propose for these POCs?

[06:12] Maya Chen: yes. generally success criteria include: 1) functional parity — outputs are semantically acceptable per your eval set, 2) latency SLOs met (p50/p95 targets you define), 3) throughput and cost targets — e.g., < $X per 1M tokens or sustain Y qps within latency SLO, 4) reliability — <1% error rate under target load, and 5) operational integration — ability to run in your VPC or adhere to security constraints. we'll draft a one-pager with these items and fill in the numeric targets based on today's numbers.

[07:00] Aaron Lee: for measuring cost, how do you account for batching and caching effects?

[07:10] Liam O'Connor: the harness logs per-token counts, batching stats, and we calculate effective cost per 1M tokens using the model runtime plus overhead. We'll run both pico-batches (low batching) and continuous batching to show delta. We'll also run KV cache enabled vs disabled to quantify improvement for repeated prefixes.

[07:40] Priya Kumar: timelines — how long does it take to get an initial baseline?

[07:48] Maya Chen: once we have your prompt set and staging access, we can run a 2-hour baseline within 3 business days. Full POC with multiple runs and analysis usually spans 2-3 weeks. For your timeline, Jordan said you want results before end of month?

[08:05] Jordan Reyes: yes, ideally mirroring our procurement window — want to present results by 12/20.

[08:15] Maya Chen: that is doable. we'll plan for an initial run next week and follow-ups.

[08:30] Liam O'Connor: a couple technical notes: streaming vs non-streaming have different instrumentation. For streaming tests we measure time-to-first-token, average chunk cadence and connection churn. For non-streaming we measure request queueing and tail latency under batching. Also note, if you use our Dedicated pools, we can pin instances to get consistent latency; hosted mode may have slightly higher variance.

[09:05] Jordan Reyes: how do you handle fallbacks/overload? e.g., if capacity hits a limit during spike.

[09:13] Liam O'Connor: Redwood supports smart routing: we can route to a lower-capacity model variant, or spill to a cheaper region with slightly higher latency, or return a degraded response. For the POC we'll measure these behaviors and show graceful degradation configs.

[09:35] Priya Kumar: any gotchas with long-seq generation and memory on the GPU side?

[09:44] Liam O'Connor: yes, long sequences impact KV cache and memory; some kernels are more efficient with quantized models. We'll capture OOM rates during the stress runs and flag model/quantization recommendations.

[10:05] Aaron Lee: for instrumentation do you require agents or only logs from the harness?

[10:13] Liam O'Connor: harness provides logs and metrics (prometheus format) you can scrape. For deeper tracing we have an optional tracing hook that spans request across service boundaries. If you want to keep things air-gapped, the harness can emit artifacts you upload for analysis.

[10:40] Jordan Reyes: is the harness repo public? can we review it before giving access?

[10:48] Maya Chen: it's internal but we'll share a read-only clone and a sanitized README with examples. link placeholder: https://repo.redwood.internal/bench-harness (we'll send access).

[11:00] Priya Kumar: regarding credentials, we prefer short-lived tokens and least privilege.

[11:07] Maya Chen: agree. we'll issue short-lived creds with a 24h TTL scoped to the staging subnet.

[11:20] Jordan Reyes: what model catalog choices will you run? we want to compare a couple open models and a Redwood verified profile.

[11:28] Liam O'Connor: we'll propose 2-3 variants: a high-throughput quantized open model, a medium-latency higher-quality model, and Redwood-verified balanced profile. We'll enumerate exact model names in the run plan. Note that some model names may be transcribed in notes weirdly, e.g., 'crowd-llm' vs 'crown-llm' — we'll be careful in the doc.

[11:58] Maya Chen: ok next steps recap — we'll: share harness repo + README, send SOC2 summary and security answers, provide a draft POC success criteria doc with numeric targets, and propose a 2-hour run next week. Jordan will share prompts and sample scripts and Priya/Aaron will provision test access.

[12:20] Jordan Reyes: sounds good. can we also have a short checklist for the engineer running the harness? like ports, docker image tags, and expected metrics output.

[12:35] Liam O'Connor: yes, we'll send a runbook with docker tags, port whitelisting (443 plus ephemeral), prom endpoint, and sample k6 commands.

[13:02] Priya Kumar: one more question: do you simulate network latency to emulate clients from our EU region?

[13:10] Liam O'Connor: yes the harness has network shaping via tc/netem or container-level proxies. We can run EU-latency profiles and show geo impact on p95.

[13:40] Aaron Lee: ok, that helps. Regarding cost — will you provide a modeled cost projection for our traffic mix?

[13:49] Maya Chen: yes, after runs we'll produce a cost model spreadsheet showing per-model cost per 1M tokens and expected monthly cost for your projected QPS distribution. We'll share a sample spreadsheet template in the repo.

[14:12] Jordan Reyes: timeline again: if we provide artifacts by EOD Tuesday, can you run baseline on Thursday?

[14:20] Maya Chen: yes we can target Thursday for the 2-hour baseline. We'll calendar a 2-hour window and ask for a Slack channel for live troubleshooting.

[14:38] Priya Kumar: any risk if we run inside our VPC? network policies might block egress for some docker images.

[14:47] Liam O'Connor: we can provide offline docker images that you can host inside your registry; harness supports that. We'll include image tarballs in the repo release.

[15:10] Jordan Reyes: excellent. is there anything else we need to agree before we wrap?

[15:16] Maya Chen: just to confirm success numeric targets: Jordan, we'll draft the one-pager with p95 <500ms for 128 tokens, sustain 200 qps non-streaming, error rate <1%, and cost threshold TBD — you'll confirm the $/1M token target.

[15:35] Jordan Reyes: agreed, i'll put the cost target in the doc early next week.

[15:50] Maya Chen: ok final logistics: i'll send the harness link, the runbook, and SOC2 summary. Liam will follow up with the staging config and streaming test plan. we'll schedule the run and set a Slack channel.

[16:05] Aaron Lee: thanks all. we'll get the prompt set and access info to you by Tuesday.

[16:18] Maya Chen: great, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with next steps and calendar invite. bye.

[51:20] (call ended)

Notes on transcript: transcription contains some imperfect proper nouns and occasional mis-attributions; speakers sometimes overlap. The technical details above are paraphrased from the call and exact model names and repo links will be provided in follow-up email.
